prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not withhold IV thrombolysis because of the aortic arch surgery 6 weeks (42 days) ago or the extracranial carotid dissection: the CTA excludes extension into the graft or the aorta.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation.
Do not perform emergent carotid endarterectomy within 48 hours.
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation without weighing recent surgical bleeding risk with the cardiothoracic team.
Do not manage recurrent transient deficits in a patient with a known carotid abnormality as outpatient observation.
Do not give antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy in the first 24 hours after IV thrombolysis, before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:00, about 3 hours before arrival; each earlier episode resolved completely) and the NIHSS (6).

IV thrombolysis: give (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, maximum 90 mg, or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg, maximum 25 mg): about 3 hours from last known well, disabling right hemiparesis (grip 2/5, unable to walk), no haemorrhage on CT, glucose 158 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 278, blood pressure 162/88 mmHg. The CTA shows the dissection entering the mid common carotid artery 7 cm beyond the graft, with the graft, its anastomoses and the native aorta free of flap or false lumen, so the aortic arch dissection contraindication does not apply; an extracranial cervical artery dissection is not a contraindication, and the operation 42 days ago is outside the 14-day major-surgery exclusion. Thrombectomy: not indicated because there is no intracranial large vessel occlusion; the deficit reflects reduced inflow and embolism through the dissected carotid.

Discuss the dissected segment with vascular surgery, cardiothoracic surgery and neurointervention: emergent endarterectomy within 48 hours is not beneficial (AHA/ASA 2026 §4.12, COR 3: No Benefit); endovascular stenting is considered if events recur despite antithrombotic therapy.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours, with post-thrombolysis neurological and blood pressure checks.

Treat the extracranial dissection with antithrombotic therapy for at least 3 months (COR 2a; CADISS and TREAT-CAD enrolled extracranial dissection), starting once imaging 24 hours after thrombolysis excludes haemorrhage: events recurred on aspirin, so start unfractionated heparin, then an oral anticoagulant, stopping aspirin while anticoagulated; aspirin plus clopidogrel is the alternative if the surgeons judge the bleeding risk too high. Check platelets at 24 hours of heparin (heparin during bypass 6 weeks ago).

Keep blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis (162/88 on arrival needs no lowering) and below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after it, but do not lower it further: perfusion of the left hemisphere depends on flow through the 80 percent true lumen stenosis; hold amlodipine and losartan for the first 24 to 48 hours unless the post-thrombolysis limit is exceeded, and avoid hypotension and dehydration.
Increase to a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) for LDL 128 mg/dL with peripheral arterial disease and diabetes; target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kenji Takahashi is a 70-year-old right-handed man who presents to the emergency department with persistent right-sided hemiparesis that began approximately three hours ago. He has a significant recent surgical history, having undergone total aortic arch replacement for a distal aortic arch aneurysm approximately six weeks prior to this presentation. His postoperative course was initially uncomplicated, and he was discharged from the surgical service two weeks after the operation in stable condition. Beginning approximately two weeks ago, he began experiencing recurrent episodes of transient right-sided weakness involving his arm and leg, each lasting between 30 minutes and several hours before spontaneously resolving. He reports approximately five such episodes over the past two weeks, each following a similar pattern with sudden onset weakness and mild slurring of speech that would gradually improve. He was seen by his primary care physician after the second episode, and a follow-up was scheduled with his vascular surgeon, but no urgent workup was initiated at that time. Today at approximately 09:00, while eating breakfast, he experienced the sudden onset of right arm weakness causing him to drop his chopsticks, followed rapidly by difficulty with his right leg and mild difficulty speaking clearly. Unlike previous episodes, the symptoms have not improved over the past three hours. His wife drove him to the emergency department, arriving at 12:05. He denies any headache, visual disturbances, chest pain, or loss of consciousness. He reports no fever, recent infection, or medication changes. His postoperative imaging at the time of his surgery had noted a finding involving the left common carotid artery beyond the vascular graft, but he was told it was being managed conservatively.
